h1:
Lopburi Food
Worth Trying at Least Once
intro: Lopburi isn't just monkeys and Narai's palace. The food here is simple but hard to stop eating — from tiny bowls of boat noodles that cost a few baht each (so you order several), to dense, fragrant custard apples in late rainy season, Thai sweets sold right outside Narai Palace, and the salted eggs coated in marl clay that have become the town's signature souvenir. We've picked out the savory dishes, the sweets, and the things to take home, with the spots locals actually go to.
chips: 🍜 Boat noodles for a few baht

blocks.html: The charm of Lopburi food is that it's cheap and easy to find within walking distance — especially the old town around Phra Prang Sam Yot, San Phra Kan shrine, and Narai Ratchaniwet Palace, where you can graze all day. We've split it into three big groups: boat noodles, the town's signature dish; old-style Thai sweets; and custard apples plus souvenirs you can take home.

If there's one dish you have to try in Lopburi, many people will tell you it's boat noodles. The town has dozens of boat-noodle shops serving small bowls with a rich, spiced broth — light enough that you order several at a time. Some places still charge in the low teens of baht per bowl, so you can eat your fill for not much more than a hundred baht.

items.name: Ayutthaya Boat Noodles ("Guay Teow Bon Mueang")
items.blurb: The shop locals call 'Guay Teow Bon Mueang' (uptown noodles), in the old town near San Phra Kan shrine and Phra Prang Sam Yot — walkable from the main sights. The broth is rich in the traditional boat-noodle style, and the small bowls make it easy to keep ordering more.
items.meta: Old town · opens around 9am · often closed Fridays

items.name: Nathaphop Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A comfortable sit-down spot with a nice setting on the road toward Khao Chin Lae. The broth is well made, with boat noodles, yen ta fo, and dry versions on offer — a good choice if you want to settle in for a proper meal rather than stand and slurp.
items.meta: Road to Khao Chin Lae · sit-down

items.name: Thong Tae Wagyu Boat Noodles, Lopburi Branch
items.blurb: Beef lovers should try this one. The draw is wagyu and premium beef in boat noodles, plus a beef hot pot. It's at Nikom intersection, about 300 m past Makro, open daily.

items.name: Pa Phon Noodles
items.blurb: A legendary budget spot — bowls in the low teens of baht that reviewers say are well worth more than the price. A genuine local shop that Lopburi people keep pinning on the map.

items.name: Air Base Bus Terminal Boat Noodles
items.blurb: A well-known spot in the air base bus terminal area, in front of the BAAC bank uptown. It's where people working nearby stop in regularly — a punchy, boat-style broth, good for lunch.
items.price: Low teens of baht per bowl

blocks.title: Tips for boat-noodle fans
blocks.html: Small boat-noodle bowls are designed to be eaten several at a time — locals often order 3–5 bowls per person. Try switching between noodle types and dark (nam tok) versus clear broth to get different flavors. Many shops open late morning and close in the afternoon, so if you're set on a famous one, get there before 1pm.

blocks.html: Lopburi custard apple (noi na) has been famous since the reign of King Rama V, earning the nickname 'noi na phra thi nang' (the royal seat's custard apple). The standout traits are large fruit with dense, sweet, fragrant flesh, grown heavily around Ban Nam Chan, Khao Sam Yot, the self-help settlement zone, and Phatthana Nikhom district. Come in season and you'll find fresh custard apples sold roadside and at markets all over town.

items: Season — custard apples are most abundant from roughly August to October. Come then for the freshest fruit at the best prices; out of season it's harder to find and more expensive.
Common varieties — there's both noi na nang (chewy flesh that peels off in segments, few seeds) and noi na fai (soft, intensely sweet flesh). Taste them side by side at a fruit stall.
Where to buy — roadside stalls around Phatthana Nikhom and Khao Sam Yot, plus the fresh markets in town, usually have fruit straight from the orchards at lower prices than the shops.

blocks.title: Picking a good custard apple
blocks.html: Choose fruit with widely spaced, full, bulging 'eyes'; press gently and it should give just slightly. If it's still firm, let it ripen another 1–2 days at room temperature. Fully ripe custard apples don't keep long, so if you're taking some home as a gift, pick fruit that isn't too ripe yet.

blocks.text: Khanom Piakpoon and Palace-Side Thai Sweets

blocks.html: Lopburi's old-style sweets cluster around the old town, especially right outside Narai Ratchaniwet Palace. Khanom piakpoon — soft, chewy coconut-topped pudding — is one of the sweets you'll find at Thai-dessert shops and markets. There's also kleeb lamduan, look choop, ba bin, takoh, and various sticky-rice toppings to choose from.

items.name: Thai Sweet Shops Outside Narai Palace
items.blurb: The zone in front of Narai Ratchaniwet Palace's gate has several Thai-dessert shops and dessert cafes selling old-style khanom piakpoon, kleeb lamduan, look choop, ba bin, takoh, and mor kaeng. Perfect to grab right after touring the palace.
items.meta: Outside Narai Palace · keep sightseeing after

items.name: Old-Style Thai Sweets, Wat San Chao Riverside Market
items.blurb: An old-style Thai-dessert stall in the riverside market, with khanom piakpoon, thua paep, khai hong, and Thai sweets made fresh the traditional way. You can eat well for under a hundred baht a head — great for grazing as you stroll.
items.meta: Wat San Chao riverside market · graze and taste

items.name: Khanom Piakpoon & Thai Sweets, Old Markets in Town
items.blurb: The fresh and morning markets in town often have homemade Thai-sweet stalls — fresh khanom piakpoon topped with coconut milk and freshly grated coconut, a cheap dessert to buy while walking the market.

blocks.text: Savory Eats in the Old Town

blocks.html: Beyond boat noodles, the old town around the train station and Wichayen Road has plenty of savory food to try — good for alternating meals while you tour Phra Prang Sam Yot, San Phra Kan shrine, and Ban Wichayen.

items.name: Khao Mok Kai, Soi Kosa (Mueang Lawo)
items.blurb: A chicken biryani shop behind the train station, with both fried and boiled chicken served alongside a rich oxtail soup. Open morning to afternoon at friendly prices — good for breakfast or lunch.

items.name: Night Market in Front of Lopburi Station
items.blurb: A dinner stroll-and-eat spot, packed with savory dishes, sweets, fruit, noodles, and snacks. Ideal if you want to eat a bit of everything in one place without spending much.

items.name: Old-Town Souvenir Shops
items.blurb: The old-town area has shops selling local souvenirs and sweets to take home — marl-clay salted eggs, Thai sweets, and seasonal fruit.

blocks.html: Before you leave, pick up the souvenirs that are unique to the town. The star is the marl-clay salted egg (khai khem din so phong) — duck eggs coated in marl clay, salt, and local ingredients before curing, which gives a rich yolk and just-right saltiness. It's a souvenir you'll mainly find made this way in Lopburi.

items: Marl-clay salted eggs — well-known makers like Mae Ban Phan Por Jor Wor and Si Sakun offer them both boiled and ready to eat in woven baskets, and raw still coated in marl clay in boxes. Prices start in the low tens of baht per box.
Custard apple (in season) — if you come in August–October, you can buy fresh orchard custard apples to take home. Pick fruit that isn't too ripe so it keeps longer.
Phatthana Nikhom honey — pure honey from apiaries in Phatthana Nikhom and Chai Badan, a long-keeping souvenir for the pantry.
Thai sweets and dried goods — local sweets and OTOP products are easy to find at souvenir shops in town and outside Narai Palace.

faq.q: What food should I try in Lopburi?
faq.a: Boat noodles are the town's signature dish and the first thing people think of — small bowls in the low teens of baht that you order several at a time. After that come dense, seasonal custard apples, khanom piakpoon and Thai sweets outside Narai Palace, and the marl-clay salted eggs that are the town's signature souvenir.

faq.q: Where should I eat boat noodles in Lopburi?
faq.a: Town has several well-known shops, like Ayutthaya Boat Noodles ('Guay Teow Bon Mueang') in the old town near San Phra Kan shrine, Nathaphop Boat Noodles, Thong Tae wagyu boat noodles at Nikom intersection, and the budget-friendly Pa Phon. Many open late morning and close in the afternoon, so go before 1pm.

faq.q: When is Lopburi custard apple in season?
faq.a: Custard apples are most abundant from roughly August to October, grown heavily around Phatthana Nikhom, Khao Sam Yot, and the self-help settlement zone. Come then for fresh fruit at good prices from roadside stalls and markets in town.

faq.q: What makes a good souvenir from Lopburi?
faq.a: Marl-clay salted eggs are the town's star souvenir, available both boiled and ready to eat and raw still coated in marl clay. There's also seasonal custard apple, Phatthana Nikhom honey, and local Thai sweets to choose from.

faq.q: What food is there in Lopburi's old town?
faq.a: Around Phra Prang Sam Yot, San Phra Kan shrine, and Narai Palace you'll find boat noodles, chicken biryani on Soi Kosa behind the train station, Thai sweets outside the palace, and dinner at the night market in front of the station — plenty to graze within a short radius.
